[lane-tern] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System, the service that turns names into addresses) answers for too long:
(1) Stale answers: if a site moves to a new address, users are sent to the old one and may see errors or outages.
(2) Slow recovery from attacks: if a false answer is cached, it keeps misleading users until it expires.
(3) Delayed failover: traffic cannot be redirected quickly to backup servers during a fault or maintenance.

[lane-tern] Idempotent (safe to repeat) retries matter because networks fail in ways that leave you unsure whether a request worked, so you must be able to send it again. If repeating a request gives the same result as sending it once, a retry cannot cause harm such as a double payment or a duplicated order.

[lane-tern] Two trade-offs of UUIDv7 (a time-ordered Universally Unique Identifier) as a primary key: (1) Size: it takes 16 bytes, which is bigger than a plain whole-number key, so indexes and joins use more storage and memory. (2) Leaked timing: the first part holds the creation time, so anyone who sees an ID can estimate when the record was made, and IDs created in the same millisecond are only loosely ordered.

[lane-tern] A write-ahead log is a file where a database records each change before it alters the main data, so the change is safely saved first. After a crash or power cut, the database replays this log to restore any lost work and to undo changes that were only half finished.

[lane-tern] (1) Fair comparison: if the client version changes between runs, any difference in results might come from the client and not from the thing being tested. (2) Repeatable results: a fixed version lets others rerun the benchmark later and get comparable figures, since updates can change speed or behaviour.

[lane-tern] Backpressure is a way for a queue to tell the senders to slow down when the receivers cannot keep up, for example by delaying or refusing new items. This stops the queue growing without limit, which could use up memory or make waiting times far too long.

[lane-tern] Two ways a scheduled job can run twice: (1) the same job is set up on two servers, so both start it at the same time; (2) a slow run is still going when the next one starts, so the runs overlap. One guard: take a lock before starting, such as a database row or a lock file, and skip the run if the lock is already held.

[lane-tern] A tombstone is a small marker left behind when an item is deleted in a store that keeps copies on several machines. Instead of simply removing the item, the store records that it was deleted, so a copy that missed the deletion does not bring the item back to life. Tombstones are cleared away after a set time, once all copies are expected to have seen them.

[lane-tern] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than truly failing: (1) It passes and fails on the same code, with no change between runs, so running it again often gives a different result. (2) The failures depend on things outside the code, such as timing, the order tests run in, shared data, or the network, and they disappear when the test is run alone. A real failure, by contrast, fails the same way every time.

[lane-tern] A lease-based lock gives a machine the lock for a fixed period, after which it expires and another machine may take it. Clock skew means two machines disagree about the current time. If the holder's clock runs slow, it believes it still has the lease after the lock service has already handed it to someone else, so two machines act at once. If a clock runs fast, a lease may seem to expire early. Safer designs add a fencing token, a rising number that storage checks, so stale holders are refused.
